source.title: Are wider nets better given the same number of parameters?
source.authors: A. Golubeva; Behnam Neyshabur; Guy Gur-Ari

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies width and parameter count in image-classification networks, but it does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, fit or test power laws, or test compute-optimal allocations. Its image accuracy results do not measure the loss named in V4 or the power-law form named in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling work and discusses parameter count, but its own experiments report image-classification accuracy and a simplified neural-network kernel analysis, not the outcomes named by the claim versions. Rows below preserve its related fixed-parameter image-accuracy results as findings outside the listed versions. The paper's plotted width curves contain additional separate results; detailed plotted points are not transcribed here.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. (2020) only as evidence that more parameters improve performance. Its own experiments measure image-classification test accuracy of statically sparse, widened ResNet-18 and MLP models at a fixed weight count. It fits no power law, measures no language-model pretraining loss, and tests no compute allocation. V4 concerns language-model loss at fixed parameter count under dense shape changes. This study changes width through random sparsity in image classifiers and reports accuracy, which is a different system, construct and measure. V5 needs a power-law form in another modality, and none is fitted. The findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Precisely: for models with random static sparsity, width rather than weight count largely determines test accuracy, provided training accuracy stays high. On ImageNet, sparse widening nearly matches dense widening. Closeness of the sparse model's GP kernel to the infinite-width kernel correlates with performance.
record.recipe_differences: Image-classification accuracy experiments that widen randomly sparsified networks at fixed weight count, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, baseline model size, widening factor, sparsity distribution, and activation function affect reported image-classification accuracy; the paper says performance declines at larger widening when training accuracy deteriorates.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet-18 and one-hidden-layer MLP image classifiers at a fixed weight count, widening via static random sparsity raises test accuracy up to a widening factor. On ImageNet the gain nearly matches dense widening up to width 181 (70.66% vs 70.91%). Accuracy then declines as sparsity degrades training accuracy. Non-linear bottleneck widening gives no gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count, width achieved through random static sparsity improves image-classifier accuracy until sparsity impairs optimization.

record.problems: The experiments concern image-classification accuracy rather than language-model pretraining loss. For ImageNet, runs were not generally repeated; the authors checked two datapoints and report variance below 0.1%. Detailed values for many width conditions are shown only in plots.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 1, 6, 7, and 9–14 contain additional plotted width, size, connectivity, and sparsity-distribution results, including separate curves for multiple baseline sizes and seeds. Their individual plotted points are not transcribed; selected table values and textual/aggregate findings are retained above.

untested.parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No compute-optimal split between parameters and tokens.
No language-model loss under depth or width changes at fixed parameter count. Only sparse widening of image classifiers, measured by accuracy.
Image models are trained, but no power-law form is fitted for any modality or training regime.
No downstream performance related to scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of scaling-law exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'discusses' is changed to 'cites_only', because Kaplan et al. appears only as a citation for the parameter-count trend. The bottleneck results (Figure 3) and the kernel-distance results (Figure 8) are not rowed. They bear on no version, so they are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
No fixed-compute language-model allocation between parameters and tokens.
The paper varies width at fixed parameter count in image classifiers, but reports accuracy rather than loss; it does not test the stated loss effect of depth, width, or other architecture details.
Image classification is studied, but no power-law loss form is tested in images or other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance relationship to language-model scale or pretraining loss is tested.
No scaling-law exponents, fit choices, or compute-optimal allocation trends are compared.
